ci-one-mean-s1.title: One-way distances of 25 bike commuters
ci-one-mean-s1.text: A city transportation office surveyed a random sample of 25 of the city's many thousands of bike commuters and recorded each one's one-way commute distance (invented data). The sample mean is $\bar{x} = 6.8$ miles and the sample standard deviation is $s = 2.9$ miles.

plot.label: Dotplot of 25 one-way bike commute distances, from 1.1 to 12.7 miles, roughly symmetric with no outliers

ci-one-mean-s2.title: Typing speeds before and after a course
ci-one-mean-s2.text: A large high school offers a keyboarding course. A random sample of 10 of this year's students in the course typed a passage on the first day and again on the last day (invented data). The table gives words per minute.

table.caption: Words per minute for 10 students, before and after the course

items.q: How many degrees of freedom does the t distribution for a confidence interval for the mean distance have?

why.correct: A one-sample t interval uses $\text{df} = n - 1 = 25 - 1 = 24$.

mistakes.why: Degrees of freedom are one less than the sample size: $n - 1 = 24$. One is used up by estimating the mean.

items.q: What is the critical value $t^*$ for a 95% confidence interval for the mean distance?

why.correct: With $\text{df} = 24$, the middle 95% of the t distribution lies between $-2.064$ and $2.064$, so $t^* = 2.064$ (Table B, df 24, 95% column, or technology: the 0.975 quantile of t with 24 df).

mistakes.why: That is $z^*$ for 95%. The population standard deviation is unknown, so the interval uses $t^*$ with 24 degrees of freedom.
That puts 5% in one tail. A 95% interval leaves 2.5% in each tail: use the 0.975 quantile.

items.q: Write the expression for the 95% confidence interval for the mean one-way distance, with $t^* = 2.064$. Type it as on the exam, for example a +/- b*c/sqrt(n).

mistakes.why: 1.96 is z*. With s in place of sigma, the critical value comes from the t distribution with 24 df: 2.064.
The standard error divides s by the square root of n: 2.9/sqrt(25), not 2.9/25.
That uses the spread of single commuters. The interval needs the standard error of the mean, 2.9/sqrt(25).

items.q: Construct the 95% confidence interval for the mean one-way distance of the city's bike commuters, in miles.

why.correct: $6.8 \pm 2.064\frac{2.9}{\sqrt{25}} = 6.8 \pm 1.197$, from 5.60 to 8.00 miles. Technology (a one-sample t interval) gives the same.

items.q: The sample has only 25 commuters. How is the normal/large sample condition met?
options: 25 is less than 10% of the many thousands of bike commuters in the city
The dotplot of the sample shows no strong skew and no outliers
The sample was chosen at random
25 is at least 10

why.correct: Normal/large sample: the population is normal, or $n \ge 30$, or (as here) a graph of the sample shows no strong skew or outliers.
options: That is the 10% condition, about independence. It does not address the shape.
With $n < 30$, check a graph of the sample: this dotplot is roughly symmetric with no outliers, so a t interval is reasonable.
That is the random condition. The normal/large sample condition is about shape or sample size.
10 is the large counts threshold for proportions. For means, either $n \ge 30$ or a graph without strong skew or outliers.

items.q: Why should the analysis use the 10 differences, after minus before, instead of the before and after values as two separate samples?
options: Each student was measured twice, so the data are paired
The after scores are higher than the before scores
The sample of 10 is too small for two samples
Differences are approximately normal by the central limit theorem

why.correct: Paired data: two measurements on the same individuals. Subtract within each pair and work with the differences, a single sample estimating $\mu_d$.
options: The two speeds come from the same student, so they are not independent samples. Paired data are analyzed through the differences, as one sample.
The direction of the change is not the reason. The design (two measurements on each student) is.
Sample size does not decide the method. Pairing does.
With 10 differences, the central limit theorem cannot be counted on; the reason to use differences is the pairing.

items.q: What is the mean $\bar{x}_d$ of the 10 differences (after minus before), in words per minute?

mistakes.why: The differences are after minus before, so faster typing gives a positive difference.
That leaves out the student whose speed fell (difference $-2$): $\frac{65}{9} = 7.22$. Average all 10 differences, including the negative one.

items.q: What is the standard deviation $s_d$ of the 10 differences, in words per minute?

why.correct: Technology (one-variable statistics on the differences) gives $s_d = 4.11$ words per minute, dividing the sum of squared deviations by $n - 1 = 9$.

mistakes.why: That divides by $n = 10$. The sample standard deviation divides by $n - 1 = 9$.

items.q: Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean change in typing speed (after minus before) for students in the course, in words per minute.

why.correct: Paired t interval: $\bar{x}_d \pm t^*\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}} = 6.3 \pm 2.262\frac{4.11}{\sqrt{10}} = 6.3 \pm 2.94$, from 3.36 to 9.24 words per minute ($\text{df} = 9$).

items.q: To check the normal/large sample condition for this interval, which graph should you make?
options: A dotplot of the 10 differences
A dotplot of the 10 before speeds
Side-by-side boxplots of before and after
A dotplot of the 20 speeds together

why.correct: With $n = 10 < 30$, the differences must show no strong skew or outliers. These 10 differences, from $-2$ to 12, show neither.
options: The procedure is a one-sample t interval on the differences, so the differences are the sample whose shape matters.
The before speeds are not the sample being analyzed.
Those compare two groups; the interval is built from one list of differences.
Mixing before and after values ignores the pairing.

items.q: Why does a confidence interval for a mean use $t^*$ instead of $z^*$?
options: The data come from a skewed population
The sample is smaller than 30
The interval uses $s$ in place of the unknown $\sigma$
By definition, intervals for means use t and intervals for proportions use z

why.correct: With $\sigma$ unknown, $\frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s/\sqrt{n}}$ follows a t distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom, which is wider than the standard normal.
options: The shape condition is separate. Even for a normal population, using $s$ calls for t.
Large samples use $t^*$ too, whenever $\sigma$ is estimated by $s$.
Replacing $\sigma$ with $s$ adds variability, because $s$ changes from sample to sample. The t distribution, with heavier tails, accounts for it.
There is a reason: for means the standard error estimates $\sigma$ with $s$, which adds extra uncertainty.

items.q: As the degrees of freedom increase, what happens to $t^*$ for 95% confidence?
options: It increases toward 3
It decreases toward $z^* = 1.96$
It stays the same, at 1.96, whatever the sample size
It decreases toward 0

why.correct: Table B: the 95% column falls from 12.71 at df 1 toward 1.96 in the infinite row.
options: The heaviest tails, and the largest $t^*$, come with the fewest degrees of freedom.
More data make $s$ a steadier estimate of $\sigma$, so the t distribution gets closer to the standard normal: 2.776 at df 4, 2.064 at df 24, 1.984 at df 100.
$t^*$ is larger than 1.96 at each finite df, and the gap shrinks as df grows.
$t^*$ approaches $z^* = 1.96$, not 0: the middle 95% of a normal curve still has width.

items.q: The 95% confidence interval for the mean one-way distance of the city's bike commuters is from 5.60 to 8.00 miles. Build the interpretation.

why.correct: The confidence is about the method capturing the parameter, the true mean distance of all the city's bike commuters, not about individual commuters or the sample mean.

options: We are 95% confident that
There is a 95% probability that
95% of the time,

why.1: The parameter is fixed; once the interval is built it either captures it or not.
why.2: Confidence describes the method over many samples, and this sentence is about one interval.

options: the interval from 5.60 to 8.00 miles captures
95% of commuters ride between 5.60 and 8.00 miles, which describes
the sample mean of 6.8 miles lies in the interval, which estimates

why.1: The interval estimates a mean, not where individual distances fall.
why.2: The sample mean is the center of the interval by construction; there is nothing to estimate about it.

options: the true mean one-way distance of all the city's bike commuters
the mean one-way distance of the 25 sampled commuters
the one-way distance of a typical commuter

why.1: The sample mean is known exactly: 6.8 miles. The interval is for the population mean.
why.2: The interval is for a mean, not for one person's distance.

conclude.model: We are 95% confident that the interval from 5.60 to 8.00 miles captures the true mean one-way distance of all the city's bike commuters.

items.q: Interpret the confidence level of the 95% interval for the mean one-way bike commute distance (from samples of 25 commuters).

why.correct: The level describes the method: the long-run share of intervals, from repeated random samples of the same size, that capture the true mean.

options: If we took many random samples of 25 commuters and built a 95% interval from each,
If we measured 95% of the city's commuters,
Since 95% of the 25 distances fall in the interval,

why.1: The level is about repeating the sampling, not about measuring part of the population.
why.2: The interval is not built to contain 95% of the data.

options: about 95% of the intervals would capture
about 95% of the sample means would equal
there is a 95% chance that this interval captures

why.1: Sample means vary; the intervals around them are what capture or miss.
why.2: That sentence is about this one interval, and the level describes many.

options: the true mean one-way distance of all the city's bike commuters
the sample mean of 6.8 miles
the distances of 95% of commuters

why.1: Every interval captures its own sample mean, its center.
why.2: The intervals estimate a mean, not individual distances.

conclude.model: If we took many random samples of 25 bike commuters and built a 95% interval from each, about 95% of the intervals would capture the true mean one-way distance of all the city's bike commuters.

items.q: A researcher records the ages of both partners in a random sample of 30 married couples and wants to estimate how much older husbands are than wives, on average. Which procedure fits?
options: Two separate t intervals, one for the husbands' ages and one for the wives' ages, then compare
A two-sample z interval for the difference of two proportions
A one-sample z interval using 1.96
A one-sample t interval for the mean of the 30 differences, husband minus wife

why.correct: Pairs: compute husband minus wife for each couple, then $\bar{x}_d \pm t^*\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{30}}$ with 29 df.
options: Two intervals do not estimate the mean of the paired difference, and they ignore the pairing.
Ages are quantitative, so this is about means, not proportions.
The population standard deviation of the differences is unknown, so use $t^*$.
The two ages in a couple belong together, so the data are paired: one difference per couple, then a t interval for $\mu_d$.

items.q: What is $t^*$ for a 90% confidence interval for a mean from a random sample of 12 observations?

why.correct: $\text{df} = 12 - 1 = 11$. A 90% interval leaves 5% in each tail, so $t^*$ is the 0.95 quantile of t with 11 df: 1.796.

mistakes.why: That is $z^*$ for 90%. With $s$ estimating $\sigma$, use t with 11 df.
That uses 12 degrees of freedom. A one-sample t interval has $n - 1 = 11$.
That is the 95% critical value. For 90% confidence, each tail holds 5%.

items.q: A random sample of 12 home sale prices in a town includes one mansion priced far above the rest, and a dotplot is strongly skewed right. Is a t interval for the mean sale price appropriate?
options: No, the skew and outlier are too strong for $n = 12$
Yes, because the sample was random
Yes, because t procedures are designed for small samples like this one
No, because 12 is less than 10% of the homes

why.correct: For $n < 30$, a t interval needs sample data without strong skew or outliers. One extreme price pulls $\bar{x}$ and $s$ a long way.
options: A small sample needs a graph with no strong skew or outliers. Here the dotplot shows both, so a t interval could be misleading.
Random sampling is one condition; the shape condition fails here.
t procedures handle unknown $\sigma$; for small samples they still need roughly normal data.
Being under 10% of the population helps (independence). The problem is the shape.
